summary: Distributed for information only, this RFC provides an alpha update of the X Window System Protocol, version 11, as of April 1987. It says the system has been widely reviewed and tested, and encourages the Internet community to experiment with it. It does not establish an Internet standard.

eli5.summary: It is the rulebook for how a program on one computer can draw windows on another computer's screen, shared with the public to try out.

subtitle: Client-server protocol for the X Window System to draw windows and handle input over the network.

tldr.problem: Graphical applications normally run directly on a display, but sometimes a programmer needs to run a graphics program on one computer and display it on another, or run many programs sharing a single display. A protocol is needed to separate the application from the display hardware.
tldr.mechanism: The X Window System Protocol defines a client-server architecture where applications (clients) connect to a display server over TCP or other reliable byte stream. Clients send requests to create windows, draw shapes, and handle input; the server sends back events (mouse clicks, keyboard presses, window exposure) asynchronously.
tldr.outcome: X became the standard windowing system for Unix and enabled distributed graphics computing. Programs run remotely but display locally, and multiple programs can share a single display with independent windows.

today: RFC 1013 is an informational distribution of the X Window System Protocol version 11 alpha update from April 1987. It does not establish an Internet Standard but documents the protocol used by X Window System implementations. X11 became the standard windowing system for Unix and remains widely used in the Unix ecosystem.

sections.title: Distributed Graphics and Protocol Overview
sections.content:
The X Window System is a software system for distributed graphics on Unix and Unix-like systems. Unlike most graphics libraries, X separates the client (the application program) from the server (the display hardware and input devices). A client runs on one machine and communicates with a server running on another machine over the network.

This RFC specifies version 11 of the X Protocol (the core protocol used for this client-server communication). The protocol was designed by Robert W. Scheifler at MIT's Laboratory for Computer Science and evolved through contributions from multiple vendors including Digital, Sun, Hewlett-Packard, and others.

The protocol is intentionally mechanism-focused rather than policy-focused: it provides low-level building blocks for window creation, graphics operations, input event handling, and resource management, but does not dictate how applications should use these mechanisms. This flexibility allows different window managers and user interface styles to be built on the same protocol foundation.

The protocol can run over any reliable byte stream (TCP for remote connections, shared memory for local), supports multiple simultaneous clients, and allows the server to maintain multiple screens (physical displays) with independent window hierarchies on each screen.
sections.eli5: X is the language that graphics programs speak to tell a display server what to draw and where. The program and the display can be on different computers. Many programs can talk to one server, each drawing its own windows.

sections.title: Messages: Requests, Replies, Events, and Errors
sections.content:
The protocol uses four types of messages. Requests are commands from client to server. Each request contains an 8-bit opcode, a 16-bit length field (in 4-byte units), and data. The server processes requests sequentially and maintains a sequence number (starting at 1) for tracking replies and errors. There are 127 core requests; opcodes 128-255 are reserved for extensions.

Replies are responses from server to client for requests that ask questions (most requests are asynchronous and do not generate replies). A reply is always 32 bytes followed by optional data, and includes the sequence number of the request it answers.

Events are asynchronous messages from server to client, always 32 bytes. Events report device activity (keyboard and mouse input), window state changes (expose, visibility, structure changes), or property changes. The server only sends events that the client has explicitly requested. A client can also send events to other clients via a SendEvent request, in which case the high bit of the event type is set to distinguish them.

Errors are 32-byte messages reporting that a request failed. The error includes an 8-bit error code, the opcode of the failed request, and the sequence number. For certain errors (such as Drawable, Colormap, Cursor), the failing resource ID is returned. Event codes 64-127 are reserved for extension events.
sections.eli5: Requests are orders the client gives the server ("draw a line"). Replies are answers ("OK done"). Events are notifications the server sends unprompted ("the user clicked here"). Errors report failures.

sections.title: Windows, Pixmaps, and Other Resources
sections.content:
The X server manages six types of resources that clients use to draw and interact. Windows are rectangular areas on the screen with borders, backgrounds, and properties. Each window has an ID (a 32-bit integer) and exists in a hierarchy: every window except the root has a parent, and windows can have children (subwindows). InputOutput windows are normal opaque windows used for drawing. InputOnly windows are invisible and used only for input control (cursors, grabs, event generation).

Pixmaps are off-screen images: three-dimensional arrays of pixels with a specified depth (bits per pixel). Graphics Contexts (GCs) hold drawing parameters: foreground/background colors, line width, font, clipping region, and how to combine new pixels with existing ones (using raster operations). A single GC can be shared across multiple drawing requests.

Fonts map character codes to glyphs (images of characters) and include spacing metrics. Colormaps are tables mapping pixel values to RGB color intensities. The server supports multiple color visual types: StaticGray (grayscale), GrayScale (indexed gray), StaticColor (indexed color), PseudoColor (indexed, modifiable), TrueColor (fixed RGB components), and DirectColor (indexed RGB components).

A Colormap is created for a specific visual type and screen. Clients allocate color cells (entries) from colormaps; some are read-only (predefined) and some are modifiable. The server can keep multiple colormaps installed on a screen simultaneously, depending on hardware limitations.
sections.eli5: Windows are boxes on the screen. Pixmaps are off-screen images. Graphics contexts are collections of drawing settings (color, line width, font). Fonts are character images. Colormaps are color palettes the server uses to display colors.

sections.title: Connecting and Negotiating Protocol Details
sections.content:
When a client connects to an X server (typically on port 6000+N for display N), it must send an initial byte indicating byte order (0102 in octal = 'B' for big-endian, 0154 = 'l' for little-endian). Following this, the client sends its protocol version, authorization protocol name and data. The server replies with success or failure, its protocol version, vendor name, release number, and a list of pixmap formats (depth and bits-per-pixel combinations), screens, input devices, and configuration limits.

The server allocates a resource ID range to each client. The client constructs new resource IDs by setting a subset of bits within the server-provided mask and OR-ing with a base value. This allows the server to distinguish resources created by different clients and reclaim them when a client disconnects.

For image data, the server specifies the byte order, how scanlines are padded and organized (XYFormat with bit planes or ZFormat with pixel values), and other format details. The server is responsible for byte-swapping protocol messages to match the client's byte order, but image data is always in the server's native format; clients must convert as needed.

Per-screen information includes the root window ID, dimensions (in pixels and millimeters), supported color depths, default colormap, white and black pixel values, and whether the server supports backing store (off-screen buffer) and save-under (background preservation). Per-visual information describes color models, RGB masks, and dynamic color modifiability.
sections.eli5: When connecting, the client and server agree on byte order and protocol version. The server tells the client which resource IDs it can use, the screen size, available colors, and what image formats it supports.

sections.title: Core Requests for Windows, Graphics, and Input
sections.content:
The protocol defines about 70 core requests. Window management includes CreateWindow (create a new window with attributes), MapWindow (make visible), UnmapWindow (hide), ReparentWindow (change parent), ConfigureWindow (move/resize), DestroyWindow (and its children). Window attributes include background/border pixmaps or colors, gravity settings (where to move contents when resizing), backing-store mode, event masks, and cursors.

Graphics requests draw on a window or pixmap using a graphics context. PolyPoint, PolyLine, and PolySegment draw points, polylines, and line segments. PolyRectangle, PolyArc, FillPolygon, PolyText8/16, ImageText8/16 draw rectangles, arcs, filled shapes, and text. CopyArea and CopyPlane transfer image data. All drawing operations use the graphics context's foreground/background colors, line attributes, and raster operation.

Input control requests manage keyboard and pointer behavior. GrabKeyboard, UngrabKeyboard, GrabPointer, UngrabPointer allow a client to take exclusive control of input devices. GrabKey, UngrabKey, GrabButton, UngrabButton enable passive grabs: when a key or button is pressed, the server switches active grab to the grabbing client. QueryKeymap returns which keys are currently pressed. SetInputFocus designates which window receives keyboard input (by default, the window containing the pointer).

Property management allows clients to attach arbitrary named properties to windows (used for communication between clients, window manager hints, etc.). GetProperty, ChangeProperty, DeleteProperty, ListProperties manage these. Colors are allocated with AllocColor (from a colormap), and colormaps are installed with InstallColormap.
sections.eli5: Requests create windows, move them, draw on them, and handle input. A client can grab exclusive control of the keyboard or mouse, or set up rules that activate a grab when a key is pressed. Clients can attach properties (named data) to windows.

sections.title: Asynchronous Events from Device and Window Changes
sections.content:
The server sends events asynchronously to report device input and window state changes. Device events report input: KeyPress, KeyRelease (keyboard), ButtonPress, ButtonRelease (mouse), MotionNotify (pointer movement). These events propagate from the window containing the pointer up the window hierarchy until a client has requested the event type, or until propagation is explicitly stopped.

Window state events report structural changes: Expose (window content lost and needs redrawing), VisibilityNotify (visibility status changed), CreateNotify, DestroyNotify, MapNotify, UnmapNotify, ReparentNotify, ConfigureNotify (moved or resized), GravityNotify (bit-gravity relocation), CirculateNotify (stacking order changed). EnterNotify, LeaveNotify report pointer entering or leaving a window. FocusIn, FocusOut report keyboard focus changes.

Coloring and property events include ColormapNotify (a colormap was installed/uninstalled) and PropertyNotify (a window property changed). SelectionNotify reports completion of a selection request (clipboard-like mechanism). ClientMessage is a generic mechanism for one client to send typed data to another.

Each window has an event mask specifying which events the client wants; the server will never send unwanted events (except errors, which are always reported). The event propagation mechanism allows a parent window to select events for its children, and children can use a do-not-propagate mask to prevent certain events from propagating up.
sections.eli5: When the user presses a key or clicks the mouse, or when windows change, the server sends events to interested clients. A client says which events it wants; the server doesn't send the rest. Events bubble up the window hierarchy until someone claims them.
